nameStory: The 'short-browed' part of this shrimp's name comes from its notably small eyestalks that barely peek out from its head, like having very short eyebrows. The 'mud shrimp' part describes where it lives and what it looks like - burrowing deep in muddy sediments along our coast.
description: Short-browed mud shrimp are small, pale crustaceans that spend their entire lives hidden in underwater burrows they dig in soft mud and sand. They're only about 1-2 inches long when fully grown, with a soft, somewhat flattened body that's perfectly shaped for their underground lifestyle. Unlike the shrimp you might see at a seafood counter, these little creatures are ghostly pale and have oversized front claws for digging. You'll almost never see one alive unless you're specifically digging for them in tidal flats.

idTips.label: Burrowing lifestyle
idTips.description: Look for small, perfectly round holes in muddy tidal flats about pencil-width across - these are the breathing holes and entrances to their deep burrows

idTips.label: Body color
idTips.description: Pale whitish or cream-colored body with a translucent, almost ghostly appearance when fresh

idTips.label: Front claws
idTips.description: Noticeably large, flattened front claws that feel sturdy and are clearly built for digging rather than pinching

idTips.label: Eye stalks
idTips.description: Very short, stubby eyestalks that barely extend beyond the head - much shorter than other local shrimp species

idTips.label: Body texture
idTips.description: Soft, somewhat squishy body that feels delicate compared to harder-shelled crabs, with a slightly rough texture from tiny scales

habitat: Found in protected muddy and sandy tidal flats along the New England coast, especially in areas with fine sediment mixed with organic matter. They prefer spots that stay consistently moist even at low tide, often near eelgrass beds or salt marsh edges where the sediment is rich and soft enough for easy digging.

seasonality.spring: Burrow activity increases as water temperatures warm, making their breathing holes more visible in mudflats during low tides.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity season when they're most likely to be found if you dig carefully in appropriate mudflat habitat during low tide.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to dig deeper as temperatures cool, so burrow holes may be less obvious.
seasonality.winter: Retreat to deeper parts of their burrows and become much less active, making them nearly impossible to find.

funFact: These tiny architects can dig burrows up to 3 feet deep - that's like a 6-foot-tall person digging a hole 300 feet down! They maintain these elaborate underground homes with multiple chambers and constantly pump water through them to breathe and filter-feed.
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other small burrowing crustaceans, but the perfectly round, smooth burrow holes are distinctive - crab holes are usually more irregular and often have little piles of sand pellets around them, while mud shrimp holes are clean and neat.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'shrimp,' these creatures are more closely related to lobsters than to the shrimp you eat, and they're sometimes called 'ghost shrimp' because of their pale, translucent appearance and secretive lifestyle.
compareHints: Since this is the only Gilvossius species in New England waters, compare it to other ghost shrimp in the same family by looking at the burrow entrance size and the shrimp's eye stalks. Short-browed mud shrimp have distinctively tiny eyestalks compared to most other burrowing shrimp species, and their burrow holes tend to be smaller and more perfectly circular.
